trivia_fact: Continuous Integration was first described by Grady Booch in his 1991 book on object-oriented design. He proposed integrating code frequently to avoid "integration hell" — the painful process of merging weeks of divergent work.

Martin Fowler wrote his influential "Continuous Integration" article in 2000 (updated 2006), establishing the key practices: maintain a single source repository, automate the build, make the build self-testing, and commit to mainline frequently.

Jenkins started life as "Hudson" in 2004, created by Kohsuke Kawaguchi at Sun Microsystems. He built it because he was tired of breaking builds on the Glassfish project and wanted automated testing before commits.

After Oracle acquired Sun in 2010, a dispute over the Hudson trademark led to a community vote in 2011. The community overwhelmingly chose to rename the project to Jenkins and fork away from Oracle. Oracle continued Hudson briefly before abandoning it.

Travis CI, launched in 2011, pioneered the hosted CI model with free builds for open-source projects. Its `.travis.yml` configuration file inspired the "CI config as code" pattern adopted by nearly every CI platform that followed.

GitHub Actions, launched in 2019, was inspired by serverless cloud functions and workflow engines. Each "action" is a reusable unit of CI/CD logic, and the YAML workflow syntax was designed to feel natural to developers already using GitHub.

The "pipeline as code" revolution — defining CI/CD pipelines in version-controlled files rather than clicking through UIs — was championed by Jenkins' Jenkinsfile (2016), though Travis CI's `.travis.yml` (2011) had already established the pattern.

Blue-green deployment was described by Daniel Bryant and others, popularized by Martin Fowler. The name simply refers to having two identical production environments (blue and green). You deploy to the inactive one and switch traffic. The color names are arbitrary.

Canary releases are named after the coal mining practice of bringing canaries into mines to detect toxic gases. The canary (small subset of users) gets the new version first — if something goes wrong, the "canary dies" before the full rollout harms everyone.

Feature flags were popularized by Flickr's engineering team around 2009 as part of their rapid deployment practice. They called them "feature flippers" — allowing code to be deployed but not activated until ready, decoupling deployment from release.

CruiseControl, built by ThoughtWorks in 2001, was one of the first dedicated CI servers. It inspired a generation of CI tools. ThoughtWorks went on to create GoCD, and Martin Fowler (a ThoughtWorks chief scientist) became CI's most prominent advocate.

Etsy became famous for continuous deployment around 2011, deploying code to production up to 50 times per day. Their engineering blog and conference talks demonstrated that rapid, frequent deployments actually reduced risk rather than increasing it.

In CI/CD, "artifact" borrows from archaeology — it's something produced (built) by the process. Build artifacts (JARs, Docker images, binaries) are stored in artifact repositories like Nexus, Artifactory, or container registries for downstream deployment.

The CI/CD principle of "shift left" testing means running tests as early as possible in the pipeline. Unit tests run first (fastest feedback), then integration tests, then end-to-end tests. This "test pyramid" concept was popularized by Mike Cohn in 2009.

Google's monorepo with trunk-based development (25,000+ engineers committing to a single main branch) proved that CI works at extreme scale. Their internal CI system, TAP (Test Automation Platform), runs billions of test cases per day.
